14. Working with lab values

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-14-labs.Rmd
book-14-labs.Rmd

What you will learn

Find a lab and its units, reduce repeated readings, present numbers without losing their meaning, and fit a model that requires an actual follow-up measurement.

You need: the Opal login from Getting started and events and reducers. This chapter uses omop.synthea, then its two-site split.

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.synthea", server = "site")$conns

Find haemoglobin and its unit 

hits <- ds.omop.concept.search("Hemoglobin", domain = "Measurement", datasources = conns)$pooled
hits[c("concept_id", "concept_name", "standard_concept")]
concept_id concept_name standard_concept
3001643 Hemoglobin and Hematocrit panel - Blood S
3004410 Hemoglobin A1c/Hemoglobin.total in Blood S
40761014 Hemoglobin.gastrointestinal.lower [Presence] in Stool by Immunoassay --1st specimen S
3011397 Hemoglobin [Presence] in Urine by Test strip S
3000963 Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood S 
lab_id <- hits$concept_id[trimws(hits$concept_name) == "Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood"]
units <- ds.omop.value.counts("measurement", "unit_concept_id", concept_id = lab_id,
  type = "both", datasources = conns)$pooled
units[c("value", "concept_name", "n")]
value concept_name n
8713 gram per deciliter 105

Choose 3000963, Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood. The recorded unit is 8713, gram per deciliter (g/dL); value holds that unit ID, and n is a record count rounded down to a multiple of five. Other haemoglobin concepts need not measure the same quantity.

Choose what one person’s number means

A unit declaration preserves the chosen unit. With the default unknown-unit rule, other-unit rows remain but their numeric values become missing; there is no automatic conversion. First and last use dates, while min and max use magnitude. All-history mean gives each reading equal weight within a person.

lab <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = lab_id, unit = omop_unit(8713L))
first <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("first_value"))
last <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("last_value"))
average <- omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("mean"))
values <- omop_recipe(variables = list(first = first, last = last, mean = average,
  minimum = omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("min")),
  maximum = omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("max"))))
recipe_execute(values, out = "D_labs", datasources = conns)
reducer_means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("first", "last", "mean", "minimum", "maximum"), function(column) {
  x <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(paste0("D_labs$", column), type = "combine", datasources = conns)$Global.Mean
  data.frame(Reducer = column, Mean_g_dl = x[1, "EstimatedMean"],
    Valid = x[1, "Nvalid"], Missing = x[1, "Nmissing"])
}))
reducer_means
Reducer Mean_g_dl Valid Missing
first 13.986 28 0
last 14.893 28 0
mean 14.467 28 0
minimum 12.746 28 0
maximum 16.104 28 0

The first-value mean is 13.986 g/dL and the last-value mean 14.893 g/dL. The mean of person means is 14.467 g/dL: each of the 28 people contributes once, regardless of how many readings they have. These first and last means use the same 28 people, so their difference, 0.907 g/dL, is their mean last-minus-first change. Three people have only one reading. The change reducer excludes those three and gives 1.016 g/dL among the 25 people with repeat readings: 0.907 × 28 / 25 (using the unrounded difference).

Keep numbers beside their groups

Grouping first and last values at the same cutoff helps compare distributions. Each row gives the number of people and the mean within that category.

grouped <- omop_recipe(variables = list(first = first, last = last,
  first_group = omop_number_bins(first, breaks = c(-Inf, 14.5, Inf),
    labels = c("below 14.5", "14.5 or above")),
  last_group = omop_number_bins(last, breaks = c(-Inf, 14.5, Inf),
    labels = c("below 14.5", "14.5 or above"))))
recipe_execute(grouped, out = "D_groups", datasources = conns)
comparison <- lapply(c("first", "last"), function(column) {
  groups <- dsBaseClient::ds.meanSdGp(paste0("D_groups$", column),
    paste0("D_groups$", column, "_group"), type = "combine", datasources = conns)
  data.frame(Number = column, Category = c("below 14.5", "14.5 or above"),
    People = as.numeric(groups$Nvalid_gp), Mean_g_dl = as.numeric(groups$Mean_gp))
})
do.call(rbind, comparison)
Number Category People Mean_g_dl
first below 14.5 16 12.650
first 14.5 or above 12 15.767
last below 14.5 10 13.120
last 14.5 or above 18 15.878

Read People as each mean’s denominator: one first or last reading per person within that category. Each pair of categories accounts for all 28 people. These cutoffs illustrate presentation; they are not clinical reference limits.

Select a nearby value and measure change

Index seven days after first haemoglobin and look back seven days. Everyone has a reading in that window by construction; the nearest reading can still differ from the first.

indexed <- omop_study(omop_index(lab, offset = 7L), outputs = "baseline",
  baseline = list(at_index = omop_value_at_index("measurement", lab_id,
    tolerance = c(-7, 0), unit = omop_unit(8713L))))
recipe_execute(indexed, out = c(baseline = "D_index"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_index$at_index", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>     5%    10%    25%    50%    75%    90%    95%   Mean 
#> 11.810 12.480 12.975 13.700 15.425 16.190 16.855 14.150
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_index$at_index", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 0

All 28 values are present. The mean becomes 14.150 g/dL because one person’s next-day reading, 11.6, replaces their first reading, 7.0. Those values belong to the public synthetic example; in a study, the protected summary alone would not identify the changed person. A narrower tolerance could leave missing values.

A slope fits value against actual date within each person. Difference is last minus first. Two eligible readings are required for change, and a slope needs distinct dates.

changes <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  change = omop_number_change(lab, "difference"),
  per_year = omop_number(omop_number_change(lab, "slope", time_unit = "days"),
    omop_number_spec(transform = omop_number_transform("affine", factor = 365))),
  target_days = omop_number_change(lab, "time_to_threshold", threshold = 14,
    op = "ge", reference = "first", time_unit = "days")))
recipe_execute(changes, out = "D_change", datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_change$change", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>     5%    10%    25%    50%    75%    90%    95%   Mean 
#> -2.940 -2.580 -1.400  1.600  2.400  3.200  3.760  1.016
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_change$change", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 3
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_change$per_year", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>          5%         10%         25%         50%         75%         90%         95% 
#> -0.26315218 -0.22388661 -0.05065106  0.08067385  0.15150943  0.28608626  0.40257901 
#>        Mean 
#>  0.05215555

There are 25 valid changes and three missing: single-reading people do not have observed change. Mean change is 1.016 g/dL. The median slope is about 0.081 g/dL per 365 days. Neither statistic implies the same change for every person, and a linear slope does not forecast a person’s next reading.

Convert, round and classify in a declared order

Target unit 8636 is gram per liter (g/L), found in chapter 6. Multiplication by ten converts g/dL to g/L. Here the conversion is applied to the person mean; an event-level omop_unit(8636L, convert = list("8713" = c(factor = 10, offset = 0))) would convert before reduction instead.

band_labels <- c("below 14", "14 to below 15", "15 or above")
presentation <- omop_number_pipeline(
  omop_number_unit("unit:8713", "unit:8636", factor = 10),
  omop_number_round("decimals", 1),
  omop_number_spec(representation = "bins", breaks = c(0, 140, 150, 1000),
    labels = c("below 140", "140 to below 150", "150 or above")))
flags <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean = average,
  rounded = omop_number(average, omop_number_spec(rounding = omop_number_round("decimals", 1))),
  band = omop_number_bins(average, breaks = c(-Inf, 14, 15, Inf), labels = band_labels),
  converted_band = omop_number(average, presentation),
  control = omop_number_category(average, range = "thresholds", thresholds = c(14, 15)),
  high = omop_number_flag(average, "ge", 15)))
recipe_execute(flags, out = "D_flags", datasources = conns)
band_means <- dsBaseClient::ds.meanSdGp("D_flags$mean", "D_flags$band",
  type = "combine", datasources = conns)
data.frame(Band = band_labels, People = as.numeric(band_means$Nvalid_gp),
  Mean_g_dl = as.numeric(band_means$Mean_gp))
Band People Mean_g_dl
below 14 9 13.341
14 to below 15 9 14.325
15 or above 10 15.607 
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_flags$converted_band",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_flags$converted_band
#>        below_140 140_to_below_150     150_or_above               NA 
#>                9                9               10                0

Both presentations give category counts 9, 9 and 10 here. The within-band means are 13.341, 14.325 and 15.607 g/dL: each person contributes their all-history mean once to their band. Bins are left-closed: 14 belongs to the middle bin and 15 to the upper bin. The bands are an ordered factor. In a model, R reports linear/quadratic terms (.L, .Q) instead of one coefficient per band. The fitted values are the same, but read the coefficients accordingly.

The equal counts do not mean rounding can never change a category. Consider a public example near the boundary:

x <- 13.996
data.frame(Input_g_dl = x, Converted_g_l = 10 * x,
  Rounded_g_l = round(10 * x, 1), Before = "below 140", After = "140 to below 150")
Input_g_dl Converted_g_l Rounded_g_l Before After
13.996 139.96 140 below 140 140 to below 150

139.96 rounds to 140.0 and crosses the cutoff. At an exact halfway value, rounding chooses an even final retained digit: 140.25 rounds to 140.2 at one decimal, whereas 140.75 rounds to 140.8. Classifying before rounding would answer a different question.

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_flags$control",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_flags$control
#>    low normal   high     NA 
#>      9      9     10      0
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_flags$high",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_flags$high
#>  0  1 NA 
#> 18 10  0

The high flag is one for 10 people. The category thresholds define low <14, normal 14–15 inclusive, and high >15, whereas the flag uses ≥15. Thus a value exactly 15 would be normal in the category but high in the flag. Synthea has no haemoglobin reference bounds; missing bounds cannot establish normality.

Pool two disjoint sites

A last value equal to first because no second reading exists is not a follow-up outcome. Index on the first lab and restrict last to days 1 onward. Use the two Synthea sites, which hold disjoint halves of the same 28 people. Log in to both as a second connection, two_conns. Its handle is named pair because omop is already attached through conns, whose tables the exercises below still use.

two_conns <- ds.omop.login(rep("https://localhost:8443", 2), user = "administrator",
  password = "password",
  server = c("north", "south"),
  resource = c(north = "omop.synthea_north", south = "omop.synthea_south"),
  symbol = "pair")$conns
followup <- omop_study(lab, outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
  first = omop_value_at_index("measurement", lab_id, tolerance = c(0, 0), unit = omop_unit(8713L)),
  last = omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", window = omop_window(1, NULL))),
  followup_days = omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce("last_date", window = omop_window(1, NULL))),
  mean = average))
recipe_execute(followup, out = c(baseline = "D_pool"), datasources = two_conns, symbol = "pair")
pooled_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_pool$mean", type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)$Global.Mean
pooled_mean
EstimatedMean Nmissing Nvalid Ntotal
studiesCombined 14.467 0 28 28

The pooled mean remains 14.467 g/dL across 28 people. Each nonmissing person receives equal weight; opening two connections to the same people would double-count them.

dsBaseClient::ds.quantileMean("D_pool$mean", type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 13.02050 13.29000 13.85104 14.28917 15.30625 15.72500 15.91000 14.46679

These are weighted averages of site quantiles, not exact quantiles of all people combined. The mean always agrees with the pooled mean because this function weights site means by their nonmissing N.

Fit a model only for people with follow-up

The model relates last to first haemoglobin only among the 25 people with a later reading. Their first and last readings are about 6–18 years apart. The summary below describes those actual intervals at each site. Each site’s length minus its missing count gives the valid values, 11 and 14, which sum to the model’s 25 complete cases. Its quantiles describe the spread, not the minimum and maximum.

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_pool$followup_days", datasources = two_conns)
#> $north
#> $north$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $north$length
#> [1] 14
#> 
#> $north$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 4056.500 4081.000 4340.000 5565.000 5853.500 5957.000 6100.500 5112.818 
#> 
#> 
#> $south
#> $south$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $south$length
#> [1] 14
#> 
#> $south$`quantiles & mean`
#>      5%     10%     25%     50%     75%     90%     95%    Mean 
#> 2177.00 2636.90 4630.50 5565.00 5570.25 6108.90 6284.95 5012.00
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_pool$followup_days", datasources = two_conns)
#> $north
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $south
#> [1] 0
fit <- dsBaseClient::ds.glm("last ~ first", data = "D_pool", family = "gaussian", datasources = two_conns)
b <- fit$coefficients["first", "Estimate"]
se <- fit$coefficients["first", "Std. Error"]
data.frame(N = fit$Nvalid, df = fit$df, Estimate = b, Lower_95 = b - qt(.975, fit$df) * se,
  Upper_95 = b + qt(.975, fit$df) * se)
N df Estimate Lower_95 Upper_95
25 23 -0.159 -0.454 0.136

The slope is about −0.159: a 1 g/dL higher first reading is associated with a 0.159 g/dL lower last reading in this small sample. Its 95% t interval, −0.454 to 0.136, includes zero. Variable follow-up and regression to the mean limit this comparison; it is not an effect of treatment or a common-time trajectory.

Exercises

1. Transform a person mean. Calculate log(mean haemoglobin). Is this the mean of that person’s logged readings?

Solution 1

logged <- omop_recipe(variables = list(log_mean = omop_number(average,
  omop_number_spec(transform = omop_number_transform("log")))))
recipe_execute(logged, out = "D_log", datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_log$log_mean", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 2.557554 2.576166 2.623579 2.661968 2.730164 2.753634 2.767809 2.669345

The median is about 2.662, the log of the median person mean, 14.325. Reduction precedes the transform: log of a mean generally differs from mean of logs.

2. Interpret observed attainment. Summarise days until the first observed haemoglobin ≥14. How do zero and missing differ?

Solution 2

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_change$target_days", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#>    0.000    0.000    0.000  185.500 2192.750 3052.000 4166.750 1274.808
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_change$target_days", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 2

There are 26 observed attainments and two missing; median time among observed attainments is 185.5 days. Zero means the first reading already meets the rule. Missing means no qualifying reading was observed; use follow-up and censoring for a time-to-event analysis rather than replacing missing with zero or discarding those people.

3. Keep a rounded copy beside the original. Request the copy from the output and summarise it. Must its overall mean have one decimal place?

Solution 3

copy <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean = average),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", columns = c("mean", "rounded"),
    number_columns = list(rounded = omop_number_column("mean",
      number_spec = omop_number_spec(rounding = omop_number_round("decimals", 1))))))
recipe_execute(copy, out = "D_copy", datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_copy$rounded", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 12.90500 13.17000 13.77500 14.30000 15.32500 15.69000 15.96500 14.45714

The overall rounded mean is 14.457 g/dL. Each person’s copy has one decimal, but averaging those values can produce more decimals. The original mean remains available for analysis; rounding does not add measurement precision.

Recap

Define the lab, unit, time window and person-level reducer before interpreting a number. Preserve missing follow-up, state threshold boundaries, and distinguish site-quantile averages from pooled person-level estimates.
